title: Now, if you want it
hook: all you pray to reach later, you can have now, if you stop refusing it (Meditations 12.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus. Your line was no thief. What choice did you make that no one could take? Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Someday, when the kids are grown. Someday, when the debt is paid off. Someday, after the promotion, after the move, after the test results come back clear. Then I'll be calm. Then I'll be kind. Then I'll really live. Book twelve is the last book of the Meditations, and its very first entry starts by taking apart that word, someday. Today, as the last book begins: now, if you want it.
screen: `SOMEDAY, WHEN.` → `THEN I'LL REALLY LIVE.` → `THE LAST BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. All the things you hope to reach by a long, roundabout road, Marcus writes, you can have now, if you don't refuse them to yourself. Second, how. Three moves. Leave the past alone. Hand the future over to providence. And set the present right, just the present, toward reverence and justice. Third, what those two words mean here. Reverence, he says, so that you love what has been given you, since nature brought it to you, and you to it. Justice, so that you speak the truth freely and plainly, and act according to law and to what each thing deserves. And don't let anything stop you: not other people's badness, not their opinions, not your own body's complaints. Fourth, the sting at the end. Then Marcus writes the line that makes this entry worth carrying. It isn't death you should fear, he says, but never beginning to live according to nature. A lot of our somedays are a way of postponing the beginning. Near the end of his notebook, Marcus says the beginning has been available all along. Not after the next promotion, the next move, the next quiet season. Now, if you stop refusing it. The life he's describing isn't waiting at the end of the road. It's at your feet.
screen: `WHAT YOU SEEK, YOU CAN HAVE NOW.` · `LEAVE THE PAST, TRUST THE FUTURE.` · `SET THE PRESENT RIGHT.` · `FEAR NEVER BEGINNING.` · then, large: `NOW, NOT LATER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look for one good thing that's already here: the chair holding you, the breath moving, a person in the next room, a quiet minute, a meal waiting. Something you usually postpone enjoying until later, until you've earned it. Let yourself have it now. Don't save it. Don't earn it first. Just receive it, fully, for this one minute, as if it were enough. The bell holds the time.
Now. Marcus opens his last book: everything you hope to reach by a long road, you can have now, if you stop refusing it. Today's word.
Your line: now, not later. When you hear yourself say someday today, ask what part of it you could have now. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often notice when they're postponing a good life until conditions change, and look for the part of it that's available today.

fork.setup: you're Marcus, near the end of your notebook. you've always thought you'd live well later, once things calm down. what does book twelve say?
options: you can have it now, if you stop refusing it.
fork.reveal: leave the past, trust the future to providence, set the present right: then what you sought by a long road is yours now.

trapdoor: what you thought: live in the moment.
what it means: what you're postponing for someday is available now, if you stop refusing it; the real fear is never beginning.
what a scholar hears: the entry divides time three ways: leave the past alone, hand the future to providence, and set only the present toward reverence and justice.

notes: 12.1 paraphrased (Long: 'All those things at which thou wishest to arrive by a circuitous road, thou canst have now, if thou dost not refuse them to thyself... if thou wilt take no notice of all the past, and trust the future to providence, and direct the present only conformably to piety and justice'; piety = being content with your lot; justice = speaking truth freely and acting by law and worth; 'it is not death that a man should fear, but he should fear never beginning to live according to nature'). Confirm.
Original νῦν: confirm 12.1 contains it near the opening.
Dating of the later books to the Danube campaigns is a common but not certain scholarly view; hedged as 'many scholars think'.

Editor review (year 2): cut the unsourced dating ('probably near the end of his life', 'after the war', 'after the reforms', the Danube campaigns in the 170s); original set to null because 12.1 appears to open on πάντα and use ἤδη ('already'), not νῦν. A Keeper may restore it as ἤδη after checking the Greek.
